content.text:
Yes. In the U.S., there are several academic/teaching areas where schools often do **not have enough qualified people willing and able to teach**, though it varies a lot by state, district, grade level, salary, and working conditions.

## K–12 fields with frequent teacher shortages

The most commonly short-staffed areas are:

- **Special education**
- **Math**, especially secondary math
- **Science**, especially physics, chemistry, and sometimes general secondary science
- **Bilingual education / ESL / TESOL**
- **Computer science / technology**
- **Career and technical education** — agriculture, trades, business, health occupations, etc.
- **World languages**
- **School support roles** like school psychologists, speech-language pathologists, and sometimes librarians/media specialists

The U.S. Department of Education maintains a national Teacher Shortage Areas database, and states submit shortage areas annually for federal purposes such as loan forgiveness eligibility. ([ed.gov](https://www.ed.gov/teaching-and-administration/professional-development/teacher-shortage-areas?utm_source=openai)) For example, Texas’s approved 2025–2026 shortage areas include bilingual/ESL, secondary CTE, computer science/technology applications, secondary English language arts, secondary math, and special education. ([sboe.texas.gov](https://www.sboe.texas.gov/texas-educators/educator-initiatives-and-performance/student-loan-forgiveness-for-teachers?utm_source=openai)) Connecticut’s 2025–2026 shortage list includes bilingual education, math, special education, science, TESOL, world languages, school library/media, and speech-language pathology. ([portal.ct.gov](https://portal.ct.gov/sde/talent_office/talent-office-home-page/shortage-areas?utm_source=openai))

## Higher-ed fields with notable teaching/faculty shortages

At the college/university level, the picture is different: there are often **many PhDs seeking academic jobs** in some fields, but shortages in fields where industry or clinical work pays much more than teaching. Examples include:

- **Nursing faculty** — a major bottleneck. U.S. nursing schools turned away tens of thousands of qualified applications because of limited faculty, clinical sites, preceptors, space, and budgets; AACN reported 65,766 qualified applications turned away in 2023, and newer AACN data reported 93,176 qualified applications not accepted in 2025. ([aacnnursing.org](https://www.aacnnursing.org/news-data/fact-sheets/nursing-faculty-shortage?sfcid=7013X000002BbcUQAS%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h826lQAA%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h82AnQAI%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h82BpQAI%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h826oQAA%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h82HZQAY%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h82CsQAI%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h82BpQAI%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h826pQAA%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h82MQQAY%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h826lQAA%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h82IWQAY%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h824PQAQ%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h82BqQAI%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h82HZQAY%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h824IQAQ%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h826pQAA%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h82MQQAY%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h82BpQAI%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h82ApQAI%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h82AnQAI%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h824JQAQ%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h826pQAA%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h826nQAA%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h824PQAQ%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h82ApQAI%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h824PQAQ%3FprogramId%3D0013X00002h82A0QAI&utm_source=openai))
- **AI / computer science instruction**, especially at institutions that cannot easily hire or retrain faculty with current AI expertise. A 2025 Computing Research Association-related paper identified faculty expertise gaps, infrastructure gaps, and curriculum-update burdens as major constraints on expanding AI education. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21713?utm_source=openai))
- **Some applied professional fields** — e.g., cybersecurity, data science, engineering technology, accounting, and health professions — depending on institution and market conditions, because qualified people can often earn more outside academia.

## Fields that are often *not* short

In many places, there is less shortage—or even strong competition—for teaching jobs in:

- **History / social studies**
- **English**, depending on region
- **General elementary education**, though this varies by state and district
- **Arts and humanities in higher education**
- Many traditional PhD fields, where there may be more qualified applicants than tenure-track jobs

So the short answer is: **yes, but shortages are concentrated in special education, STEM, bilingual/ESL, CTE, languages, and certain clinical/applied higher-ed fields—not evenly across all academic subjects.** Also, “not enough people trying to teach” is often really “not enough qualified people willing to teach under the pay, workload, location, and working conditions offered.”
